pending_items.title: ‘I cannot go to work’: Iranians contend with pollution as well as US war
pending_items.content:
Tehran, Iran – The headaches, shortness of breath and blurred vision which Ghoral, 40, a Tehran resident, once only experienced during the heavily polluted, cold seasons of the year have become year-round symptoms.

“The nausea hit me even before the Meteorological Organization announces that the air is polluted,” he tells Al Jazeera.

“On heavily polluted days, I try to leave the house as little as possible, which means I sometimes cannot go to work, affecting my income. At the same time, air pollution increases the cost of seeing a doctor and buying the medication I need to manage my breathing problems. All of this is happening simply because I have no choice but to live in a polluted city.”

The threat of American bombs is not the only danger the residents of Iran’s capital city must contend with these days: checking the air quality has become part of everyone’s daily routine.

Weather apps are no longer used primarily to check the forecast for rain or thunderstorms, but rather to view the latest readings on fine particulate matter (PM2.5) – the tiny, airborne particles which can be deadly when breathed in over a prolonged period.

Hossein, 36, a resident of the capital, tells Al Jazeera: “For someone like me, who both lives and works in the city centre, air pollution is no longer just a part of life; it has become life itself.”

There is little anyone can do about it except escape the city as often as possible, particularly during the winter months when pollution is at its worst.

“At the very least, I try to spend my weekends in nearby cities where the air quality is better,” Hossein says.

The second half of the year in Iran has traditionally been a time of what is known as “temperature inversion”. This occurs when a layer of warm air traps cooler air and pollutants close to the ground, preventing them from dispersing.

While pollution has become a year-round problem, it is particularly bad in the winter, when this phenomenon is common, bringing prolonged periods of polluted air to cities and industrial areas.

Other major Iranian cities, including Mashhad, Isfahan, Shiraz, Tabriz and Ahvaz, are also grappling with air pollution.

For more than half of the autumn and winter months, air pollution warnings are regular, advising people with heart and respiratory conditions to take precautions. Children, older people and pregnant women are also advised to stay indoors and avoid outdoor activities.

In Iran, the Meteorological Organization uses a “yellow weather warning” to signal days on which air pollution levels are particularly high. On those days, schools typically cancel outdoor physical education classes.

When pollution levels approach the threshold for an “orange weather warning” – generally associated with an air quality index (on a scale of 0-500) above 140 – additional restrictions may follow. Some employees switch to remote work, traffic restrictions under the odd-even licence plate scheme are imposed to reduce the number of cars on the streets, schools are closed and some university classes move online.

Dr Hadi Yazdani, who works at a medical centre in Isfahan, tells Al Jazeera: “One of the first signs of rising air pollution is an increase in hospital visits by patients with chronic asthma and other respiratory conditions.”

According to figures from the Ministry of Health, hospital visits for these conditions, as well as for heart conditions, rise by as much as 50 percent in the winter. Eye and skin problems also tend to become more common as a result of air pollution.

“Children and older people are particularly vulnerable,” says Yazdani. “They may develop new illnesses or experience a worsening of existing conditions. In addition, because air pollution reduces the circulation of fresh air, respiratory infections such as influenza and COVID also become more prevalent.”

Evidence that hospitals across Iran experience a surge in emergency department visits as a result of air pollution has prompted the country’s Emergency Medical Services Organization to adopt different plans for managing patient demand during the colder months.

As pollution levels worsen, specially equipped buses are deployed in public squares in some of Iran’s major cities. They provide basic treatment for less severe pollution-related conditions, such as shortness of breath and chest pain. The buses are intended both to reduce the need for ambulances to travel across congested cities and to serve as the first point of contact for people seeking medical assistance.

This year, amid concerns that a renewed war with the United States could force schools to close again anyway, the Ministry of Education has also decided to delegate decisions about school closures due to air pollution to local education authorities.

Although air pollution in Iran is caused by both natural events, such as dust storms, as well as industrial and human-made sources, Iran’s Department of Environment has focused its efforts on tackling pollution caused by human activity.

Ahmad Taheri, head of the National Center for Air and Climate Change at the Department of Environment, tells Al Jazeera: “Alongside efforts to improve the standards of petrol and diesel used by vehicles, we are putting pressure on car manufacturers to produce vehicles that meet higher standards. We are also working to reduce gas flaring at refineries, which contributes both to air pollution and global warming.”

However, the efforts of Iran’s environmental authorities have done little to reassure the public about the country’s air pollution problem.

Every year, as concentrations of air pollutants rise and public health concerns mount, advertisements for vitamins and fresh food products marketed as protective against the effects of air pollution have become increasingly common.

But Yazdani says there is little substantial research demonstrating that vitamins can reduce the health effects of air pollution. He notes that people tend to experience more mood-related problems on polluted days and believes that advertisers are capitalising on public anxiety about the impact of air pollution on health.

The World Health Organization estimates that 99 percent of the world’s population lives in places where air quality falls below the levels it recommends. Knowing this, however, does little to ease people’s concerns about the toll that air pollution is taking on their physical and mental health and Iranians are turning to anything they can find that might help.

pending_items.title: Under-attack Palestinians find unlikely ally in Israeli retired general
pending_items.content:
The four Israeli soldiers stepped out of their car in the occupied West Bank, their faces masked, their uniforms unmarked and automatic weapons strapped across their shoulders.

They had entered a Palestinian olive grove but, little did they expect, the person there planning to tell them to leave could have once been issuing them orders.

A retired Israeli general, Eyal Ben Reuven, had come that day to the Palestinian town of As Sawiyah, on a mission to prevent some of the rampant violence against Palestinians by extremist Israeli settlers.

For the 72-year-old, joined by fellow battle-hardened veterans of the Israeli military, the violence is a stain on the institution in which they once served.

"I've fought in a number of wars. And unfortunately, I have reached the point where I have seen an evolution," said the former military man with piercing eyes, who spent much of his career driving tanks.

The army is failing to act, he said, even when the violence has reached a level "I never could have imagined".

Unrest has soared in the West Bank since the unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel, which responded with a massive military campaign in the Gaza Strip.

More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by the army or settlers in the West Bank since then. More than 50 Israelis have died in the same time in the territory, which Israel captured in 1967.

The olive harvest has become a flashpoint, with settlers attacking or stealing from Palestinian farmers on a nearly daily basis.

With the other former soldiers, Ben Reuven has set up a protective presence, a tactic more common among leftist activists who put themselves in the way in a bid to stop attacks against Palestinians.

Clad in comfortable hiking attire and carrying walking sticks, it is difficult to imagine that some of the greying volunteers fought in intense combat.

Like good soldiers, they review instructions upon going out -- they are there to assist the olive harvest, not to confront the settlers, and they will obey the army's instructions.

A Palestinian human rights activist, Arafat Abu Ras, led the military men to a small olive grove. An old Palestinian woman was waiting to guide them and the soldiers, more accustomed to the battlefield than to farming, used sticks and small rakes to start knocking the olives off the trees, volunteering to do the work on the Palestinians' behalf.

Almost immediately a military vehicle arrived. Under the humming of a drone, one of the serving soldiers shoved aside an AFP team to prevent filming, while another checked Abu Ras's identity papers and ordered everyone to leave.

Abu Ras said that the olive farmers had coordinated with the army, which insists that Palestinians receive approval for their harvests in the occupied West Bank, arguing that it is for safety reasons.

"They say, 'yes, yes', and then the next day they come and force us to leave," Abu Ras said.

After the serving soldiers arrived, a second vehicle came, this time with Israeli settlers. An official from a neighbouring settlement also ordered the olive pickers out, with troops saying it was a "closed military zone".

The Israeli veterans, in line with their guidance, complied. They instead moved elsewhere with the farmers, hoping to prevent attacks on them.

"Our army is a joke," fumed Yoel Feldschuh, a 77-year-old former air force brigadier general.

"Is it its role to shut an olive grove? What does the military have to do with that?"

Feldschuh made headlines when he was handcuffed and taken away by police in a similar action a month earlier.

Changing the behaviour of the military, he said, "will take a generation".

COGAT, the Israeli body responsible for civil affairs in the Palestinian territories, maintains that "security forces are deployed to ensure a safe olive harvest".

But since September, the harvest has been marked by nearly 500 attacks, some of them fatal, according to the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din.

Amram Mitzna, an 81-year-old retired general, attributes the army's inaction to the young ages of the soldiers, who have grown up under now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader.

"They consider every Arab an enemy who must be treated as such," said Mitzna, who has also served as mayor of Haifa, Israel's third largest city.

Netanyahu has allied himself with the far-right and championed a rapid growth of West Bank settlements, which are considered illegal under international law.

Netanyahu is fighting for political survival after losing ground in elections. Gadi Eisenkot, a former general seeking to succeed him, supports many of Netanyahu's security policies but accuses him of yielding to "Jewish terrorism" in the West Bank and vowed to crack down on extremist settlers.

In As Sawiyah, the former soldiers eventually finished harvesting the olives in a nearby area alongside a school, putting them in bags to be taken by Palestinian villagers.

While no one was injured, Ben Reuven remained deeply disturbed by how the young soldier acted during the altercation.

"When I saw him arrive, masked, shouting, kicking sacks of olives, I was ashamed."

pending_items.title: In Israel, calls for 'unity' are a code for Jewish tribal supremacy
pending_items.content:
The saying “when fascism comes to America, it will be wrapped in a flag and carrying a cross” is commonly attributed to American novelist and playwright Sinclair Lewis.

German writer Thomas Mann , himself a Nobel laureate in literature, had a slightly different version: “If ever fascism should come to America, it will come in the name of freedom.”

Former Republican President Ronald Reagan, meanwhile, offered his own version : “If fascism ever comes to America, it will come in the name of liberalism.”

Whatever form fascism may take when it arrives in the US , one thing can be said with certainty: in Israel , it arrived in the name of unity.

It is hard to think of a word in the Hebrew language that has been more shamelessly abused than “unity” by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s inciting, divisive gang.

Take, for example, Elisha Madan, the newly elected Likud MK who has set up a “Unity Tent” outside the Knesset. “I intend to sit in the tent day and night, in the cold and rain, to give voice to the many people who keep reaching out to me, yearning for unity,” he declared poetically.

This great champion of unity, it is worth recalling, helped establish the settlement of Avigail . He was also filmed hurling vile slurs at the late human rights activist Ezra Nawi, who had come to the area to protect Palestinian residents from settler violence.

Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, the man who warned before the election that a left-wing government would pose an existential threat to the state of Israel, suddenly remembered after the vote to reach out to his “Jewish brothers” with a call for unity.

Amir Ohana - the former Knesset speaker who boycotted the swearing-in ceremony of Supreme Court president Yitzhak Amit, and who refused to allow bereaved families into the Knesset gallery during a Netanyahu speech about the 7 October attacks, instead having them forcibly removed - also professes to see unity as a cherished goal, with the 26th Knesset holding the means to achieve it.

The use of the term 'the people of Israel' is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging

And this week, comedian Guy Hochman shoved a camera rudely into MK Ahmad Tibi’s face, shouting at him: “Ahmad, unity? Unity?” This knight of unity is the same man who found the genocide in Gaza particularly amusing , and a fitting backdrop for a stand-up performance intended to boost the morale of the forces of destruction and annihilation.

He is also the same comedian who attended a left-wing demonstration and declared that its participants were “scarier than Qatar ”. Now, he too wants unity .

It is easy to dismiss the unity tantrum gripping Netanyahu’s camp as a cynical ploy, designed to neutralise the meaning of its electoral defeat and spare its members the prospect of being banished to the opposition benches.

But the truth is that it rests on something much deeper, rooted in the anomaly of Israeli politics: a political landscape divided not primarily along ideological lines, but above all, over the question of support for Netanyahu.

Remove Netanyahu himself from the equation, and the common ground between the two blocs is far greater than it might appear; on many issues, their areas of agreement actually outweigh their differences.

A call for unity between two blocs that stood firmly together around the most defining event in Israel’s history since its founding - the perpetration of genocide against a besieged and defenceless Palestinian population - is not entirely baseless.

But the foundation of this call for unity runs even deeper than a consensus on any particular policy. It concerns the most instinctive sense of belonging shared by members of both blocs: who they mean when they say “we”.

The Israeli right long ago replaced the concept of “Israeli citizens” with the tribal notion of “the people of Israel” - a term that clearly refers exclusively to the Jewish collective . This dangerous substitution is no longer confined to the right.

“The people of Israel cannot trust Netanyahu when he claims his motives are not political … We must not allow him to exploit Israel’s security to disrupt the elections,” Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, tweeted about a month before the election.

The distinction between “the people of Israel” and “Israeli citizens” is anything but semantic. It reflects two fundamentally different conceptions of the Israeli collective, only one of which includes Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Why did Golan choose to invoke “the people of Israel” rather than “Israeli citizens”? Are Arab citizens of Israel not equally affected by security concerns? Do they not flee to bomb shelters - when such shelters are available to them - during wartime?

The use of the term “the people of Israel” is no accident. It is a code word, an effective shortcut for establishing a shared sense of tribal belonging and manufacturing intimacy.

When Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot tells a former Likud voter, disillusioned with Netanyahu, during an election campaign that “as far as I’m concerned, there is no way the people of Israel will not prevail,” he knows exactly what he is doing: building a sense of tribal intimacy whose boundaries are perfectly clear to both men.

It is within those boundaries that the right is now calling on him to gather under its unity campaign - boundaries that necessarily leave Arabs on the outside.

It is hardly surprising, then, that the Arab parties are the only ones presenting a civic discourse as a substantive alternative to the Jewish tribal discourse embodied in the phrase “the people of Israel”.

Here lies one of the great paradoxes of the Zionist state. Since its founding, Israel has relentlessly sought to sever the connection between Arab citizens and their Palestinian national identity, subjecting them to a process of forced “Israelisation”.

Yet the moment Arab citizens seek to give real substance to the citizenship imposed upon them after the Nakba , “the people of Israel” are quick to reclassify them as Palestinians and push them back beyond the boundaries of the Israeli collective. This is the declared position of at least two of the four parties that make up the so-called change bloc.

The choice now facing Eisenkot is not merely between two different governing coalitions. It is a choice between two fundamentally different conceptions of the boundaries of Israeli citizenship: between “the people of Israel” and the citizens of Israel. If he chooses the former, he will become, under cover of the “unity” discourse, a pale appendage of a fully fledged Jewish-supremacist coalition.

If he chooses the latter, he will have to accept Arab citizens as full partners in Israeli citizenship, with an equal and legitimate stake in shaping the country’s character - rather than as people whose struggle is limited to securing whatever crumbs the state is willing to throw their way.
